--- TEXT ---
Scientific knowledge is best understood as provisional and fallible because the history of science repeatedly shows that even the most successful and well-confirmed theories are not immune to substantial revision. Newtonian mechanics, for centuries the paradigm of scientific achievement, explained planetary motion, terrestrial mechanics, tides, projectiles, and engineering phenomena with extraordinary precision. Yet it was eventually shown to be only a limiting case of deeper frameworks: special relativity revised its concepts of space, time, mass, and simultaneity at high velocities, while general relativity replaced Newtonian gravitation with the curvature of spacetime and explained phenomena such as the anomalous precession of Mercury and the bending of light. Newtonian mechanics was not simply discarded as useless; rather, it was reinterpreted as approximately valid within a bounded domain, especially at low speeds and weak gravitational fields. Classical thermodynamics likewise achieved remarkable empirical success in describing heat, work, entropy, engines, and macroscopic equilibrium processes, but its concepts were later deepened and transformed by statistical mechanics, kinetic theory, and quantum theory. What had appeared to be strict macroscopic laws came to be understood in probabilistic and microphysical terms, with their scope limited by assumptions about large numbers of particles, equilibrium conditions, and the neglect of fluctuations. These episodes show that scientific success does not amount to final certainty. The rational lesson of scientific history is fallibilism: even theories supported by vast bodies of evidence may later be revised, restricted, reinterpreted, or embedded within broader theories.

The Duhem-Quine thesis further supports the provisional character of scientific knowledge by showing that no single hypothesis is tested in complete isolation. An experimental prediction always depends on a network of assumptions, including background theories, measurement procedures, instrument reliability, mathematical idealizations, boundary conditions, and auxiliary hypotheses about the experimental setup. When an observation conflicts with a prediction, the failure does not logically identify one unique culprit. Scientists may revise the central hypothesis, but they may also adjust an auxiliary assumption, question the calibration of an instrument, refine the model of initial conditions, alter assumptions about interfering causes, or modify background commitments. This means that experimental results do not conclusively falsify individual claims by themselves. They acquire evidential force only within an interconnected web of theoretical and practical commitments. Scientific knowledge is therefore irreducibly holistic: the unit of empirical assessment is not a single isolated proposition but a larger system of mutually supporting assumptions. Because any component of that system may in principle be reconsidered in light of recalcitrant evidence, scientific claims remain defeasible. They can be powerfully supported, pragmatically indispensable, and explanatorily fruitful, but they do not become immune to revision in the manner of established certainties.

The underdetermination of theory by evidence gives a further reason to treat scientific knowledge as provisional rather than certain. Any finite body of data is compatible with indefinitely many theoretical frameworks, because the same observed regularities can be represented by different mathematical structures, interpreted through different ontologies, or extended into unobserved domains in divergent ways. A finite dataset constrains acceptable theories, but it does not logically entail a single unique theory. Multiple frameworks can fit the available evidence while differing in their accounts of hidden mechanisms, causal structures, unobservable entities, or predictions outside the range so far tested. Empirical confirmation is therefore always partial: evidence can make a theory more credible, more coherent with established inquiry, and more successful in prediction and explanation, but it cannot by itself transform that theory into an unquestionable certainty. Claims of certainty exceed what finite evidence can justify, because they assume that no future evidence, reinterpretation, or alternative framework could alter the standing of the theory. The most defensible conception of scientific knowledge is thus not as a finished inventory of indubitable truths, but as a disciplined, evidence-responsive, corrigible body of understanding whose claims remain open to refinement, limitation, and revision.
